EXHIBIT A

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; PANAYIOTA SOURAS, also known as YIOTA G. SOURAS, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

PLAINTIFF’S PROPOSED SECOND AMENDED COMPLAINT

DEMAND FOR JURY TRIAL

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT

•	On July 4, 2022, Meta Platforms, Inc. invoked its Child Sexual Exploitation policy against my Facebook account and cut off the contracts I performed through it. I sued them in September 2025. Meta filed a motion to dismiss. Meta did not staple a CyberTipline report to the motion.

•	When Meta’s co-defendants’ lawyers asserted that a “legitimate violation by Ballentine is consistent with the facts” while repeatedly putting my name beside the words “child sexual exploitation” in their papers, I sued them in February 2026. Defendants filed motions to dismiss. Defendants did not staple a CyberTipline report to their motions.

•	I sent Advanced Notice of Intended Subpoenas to NCMEC in April concerning those two cases, and their attorney, Ms. Hall, sent me two letters associating my full legal name, “Marvelle J. Ballentine,” with two CyberTipline reports. I sued them in May 2026 because I have never even used my full legal name to operate any social media account. NCMEC and Hall filed motions to dismiss. NCMEC and Hall did not staple a CyberTipline report to their motions.

•	I served Meta on July 31, 2026 concerning its role in the drafting, transmission, and delivery of the letters. It filed a motion to dismiss. Once again, it did not staple a CyberTipline report to the motion. Meta substituted the CyberTipline report with a chronicle of my prior lawsuits, their captions, and their procedural history.

•	I have sworn that I never used my full legal name to create, register, identify, maintain, access, or operate any account on any Meta product or service that I used. The defense may move to dismiss this complaint. Whether or not they staple a CyberTipline report to the motions is to be determined.

•	That matters because the two letters signed by Hall on behalf of NCMEC stated:

“In response to your subpoena issued April 9, 2026, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (‘NCMEC’) provides its written responses as detailed below.

NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the present.”

•	So, that leaves the remaining questions up for determination: Where did my legal name come from? How and why did it arrive on those letters? Did either of the two asserted CyberTipline reports, as originally received by NCMEC, actually identify “Marvelle J. Ballentine”? Did Meta submit either report? Why did NCMEC and Hall act before formal service? Why did they not wait the five days until April 27, when one court temporarily stayed discovery, or the nine days until May 1, when discovery in the other action was temporarily stayed? Where did the urgency come from?

•	I bring six counts: conspiracy under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) and Virginia law against all Defendants, for letters sent to frighten me out of my own lawsuits; defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and insulting words against Hall and NCMEC, for what the letters said and to whom. This Complaint adds NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer, Panayiota Souras, who, on information and belief, approved the wording of the letters and authorized Hall to send them before formal service. The defamation and insulting-words counts are also asserted against Souras; Count III remains against Hall and NCMEC.

JURISDICTION AND VENUE

•	This Court has subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1343(a)(1). Count IV arises under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2).

•	This Court has supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) over the claims for defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, common-law conspiracy, and insulting words. Those claims arise from the same nucleus of operative fact as Count IV: the preparation, approval, issuance, transmission, and publication of the April 22, 2026 letters. They form part of the same case or controversy.

•	In the alternative, this Court has original jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(1) over Counts I, II, III, V, and VI if complete diversity exists. Plaintiff is a citizen of the State of Florida. NCMEC, a District of Columbia non-profit corporation with its principal place of business in Virginia, is a citizen of the District of Columbia and Virginia. Meta, a Delaware corporation with its principal place of business in California, is a citizen of Delaware and California. At all relevant times, Hall and Souras worked at NCMEC’s headquarters in Alexandria, Virginia. On information and belief, each is domiciled in, and therefore is a citizen of, a State other than Florida. Plaintiff cannot presently allege the citizenship of John/Jane Does 1-6, whose identities are unknown. This basis applies only if no Defendant is a citizen of Florida and each Doe Defendant’s citizenship is alleged or no Doe Defendant remains a party. The amount in controversy exceeds $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs.

•	Venue is proper in this district under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b)(2). A substantial part of the events giving rise to the claims occurred here. Hall prepared or approved, signed, and issued the April 22, 2026 letters from NCMEC’s office in Alexandria, Virginia, within the Alexandria Division of this district. The letters were transmitted to Plaintiff’s commercial mail-receiving address in Alexandria, Virginia, where they were opened and processed.

•	This Court has specific personal jurisdiction over Hall under Virginia Code § 8.01-328.1(A)(3). Hall performed the challenged acts in Virginia. She prepared or approved, signed, issued, and caused the transmission of the April 22, 2026 letters from NCMEC’s Alexandria headquarters. The first third-party publication alleged in this Complaint occurred in Alexandria, when the commercial mail-receiving agency opened, reviewed, and scanned the letters. Each claim against Hall arises from her Virginia conduct.

•	This Court has specific personal jurisdiction over Souras under Virginia Code § 8.01-328.1(A)(3). Souras served as Chief Legal Officer of NCMEC at its Alexandria, Virginia headquarters. On information and belief, Souras reviewed, approved, and authorized the April 22, 2026 letters in the course of her work for NCMEC, and the letters issued from NCMEC’s Alexandria office and were transmitted to Plaintiff’s Alexandria address as a result. Each claim against Souras arises from that Virginia conduct.

•	This Court has general personal jurisdiction over NCMEC, a corporation with its principal place of business in Alexandria, Virginia. This Court also has specific personal jurisdiction over NCMEC under Virginia Code § 8.01-328.1(A)(3). The April 22, 2026 letters were prepared or approved, signed, and issued from NCMEC’s Alexandria headquarters, and each claim against NCMEC arises from that Virginia conduct.

•	This Court has specific personal jurisdiction over Meta Platforms, Inc. under Virginia Code § 8.01-328.1(A)(3) and the conspiracy-based attribution of forum contacts. Sections O through R allege the conspiracy. Meta knowingly participated through one or more authorized representatives or intermediaries. NCMEC and Hall committed the Virginia acts alleged in this Complaint in furtherance of that conspiracy. Meta received the April 9, 2026 materials directed to NCMEC’s Legal Department in Alexandria, Virginia. The understanding alleged in Section O contemplated that Hall would issue the case-specific correspondence from that Virginia office. Plaintiff’s claim against Meta arises from those Virginia acts.

•	The exercise of personal jurisdiction over each Defendant comports with the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

PARTIES

•	Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine, also known as Jay Ballentine, is an adult citizen of the State of Florida. At all relevant times Plaintiff maintained a mailing address at 1520 Belle View Blvd, Ste. #5847, Alexandria, Virginia 22307. A commercial mail-receiving agency operates that address and is authorized to receive and process mail on Plaintiff’s behalf.

•	Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”) is a District of Columbia non-profit corporation. Its principal place of business is 333 John Carlyle Street, Suite 125, Alexandria, Virginia 22314. NCMEC operates the CyberTipline under federal authorization in connection with 18 U.S.C. § 2258A. At all relevant times NCMEC employed Defendant Katie Hall as its Corporate Counsel. Hall was responsible for legal correspondence NCMEC issued in response to claimed legal process. NCMEC is sued for its own conduct, undertaken through Hall and one or more additional personnel. NCMEC is also sued vicariously for the conduct of Hall and Souras within the scope of their employment.

•	Defendant Katie Hall is an individual. At all relevant times she served as Corporate Counsel of NCMEC at 333 John Carlyle Street, Suite 125, Alexandria, Virginia 22314. On information and belief, Hall is domiciled in a State other than Florida and is a citizen of that State. Hall prepared or approved, signed, issued, and caused the transmission of the April 22, 2026 letters. Hall is sued individually for her own tortious conduct.

•	Defendant Panayiota Souras, known publicly as Yiota G. Souras, is an individual. At all relevant times she served as Chief Legal Officer of NCMEC at 333 John Carlyle Street, Suite 125, Alexandria, Virginia 22314. On information and belief, Souras is domiciled in a State other than Florida and is a citizen of that State. Souras was responsible for NCMEC’s legal affairs, including litigation and compliance, and managed NCMEC’s legal operations. Souras is sued individually for her own alleged participation in reviewing, approving, and authorizing the April 22, 2026 letters.

•	Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”) is a Delaware corporation with its principal place of business in Menlo Park, California. Meta was a defendant in the 376 Action and in the 286 Action, each identified in Section A, at all relevant times. Meta is an electronic service provider subject to the reporting duties of 18 U.S.C. § 2258A.

•	Meta owns and operates Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp.

•	Defendants John/Jane Does 1-6 are persons not yet identified who participated in the communications, authorization, approval, preparation, or transmission alleged in this Complaint. Their roles include: the Meta representative or representatives who communicated with NCMEC concerning Plaintiff, the identifiers, the intended subpoenas, or the two federal actions; any Accenture representative who knowingly joined or implemented the understanding alleged in this Complaint; any NCMEC personnel, other than Hall and Souras, who approved the issuance of the April 22, 2026 letters; and any intermediary, including counsel or other agents acting for Meta, Accenture, or NCMEC, through whom the alleged communications occurred. Meta, Accenture, NCMEC, and their representatives hold the records that identify the Doe Defendants. Plaintiff will seek leave to amend when those identities are ascertained.

SCOPE OF ALLEGATIONS

•	This Complaint predicates no liability on the filing of any motion, brief, or other paper in any court. Court filings identified here are alleged solely as facts establishing timing, notice, knowledge, coordination, and admissions. The claims do not challenge NCMEC’s receipt, maintenance, or lawful referral of CyberTipline reports. The claims challenge the extra-judicial agreement alleged below and the preparation, approval, issuance, transmission, and publication of external legal correspondence that falsely invoked compulsory process and served the litigation-directed purposes alleged below. No claim against Meta seeks liability for the July 4, 2022 account-level enforcement, for any content-related decision, for any failure to restore Plaintiff’s account, or for any treatment of third-party content. Those matters are alleged only to establish the subject matter of the pending federal actions, Defendants’ knowledge, Meta’s interest in whether a CyberTipline report exists, and the testimony Defendants sought to deter. The same is true of the memorandum, motion to stay, and opposition filed in the 1341 Action and the August 13, 2026 filing in the 376 Action, each identified in Section P. Each is alleged as an admission and as a fact establishing timing, coordination, and knowledge. None is conduct on which any claim rests.

FACTS

A.	The Federal Proceedings and Plaintiff’s Role as Party and Prospective Witness

•	Plaintiff filed Ballentine v. Accenture LLP, et al., Case No. 6:26-cv-00286-AGM-DCI (M.D. Fla.) (the “286 Action”), on February 9, 2026. Plaintiff filed Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., et al., Case No. 6:26-cv-00376-AGM-DCI (M.D. Fla.) (the “376 Action”), on February 17, 2026. Each action was pending in a court of the United States at all relevant times.

•	The defendants in the 376 Action included Meta, Accenture, TaskUs, Inc., and Genpact Limited. Accenture is a limited liability partnership that provides platform policy enforcement services to Meta. The defendants in the 286 Action included Meta, Devin S. Anderson, and Christopher W. Keegan. Kirkland & Ellis LLP (“Kirkland”) represented Anderson and Keegan. Accenture, Anderson, Keegan, TaskUs, Inc., Genpact Limited, Kirkland, Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP (“Orrick”), Diana M. Fassbender, and Marianna Chapleau are not defendants here. Their conduct is alleged only to establish chronology, notice, knowledge, or the conduct of the Defendants, including the Doe Defendants.

•	Both actions arise from one event. On July 4, 2022, Meta issued an account-level enforcement notice against Plaintiff’s Facebook account. That notice interrupted Plaintiff’s ability to perform third-party contracts through the account.

•	Plaintiff proceeded pro se in both actions. Every act of prosecution depended on Plaintiff’s personal capacity and participation: discovery, deposition examination, briefing, and appearance.

•	Plaintiff was a prospective witness in both actions. He expected to testify under oath, at deposition and at trial, concerning his account history, the July 4, 2022 enforcement event, the absence of any law-enforcement contact with him, and his damages.

•	The dockets of the 376 Action and the 286 Action were publicly accessible through the federal Public Access to Court Electronic Records system.

B.	The Contested CyberTipline Question

•	One question has been contested since October 2025: whether Meta, or any person acting in connection with the July 4, 2022 account-enforcement event, transmitted a CyberTipline report under 18 U.S.C. § 2258A concerning Plaintiff or his account identifiers.

•	Before April 22, 2026, no CyberTipline report concerning Plaintiff had been identified, produced, or attributed to any provider in any forum.

•	Plaintiff’s first substantive act in the 376 Action was a motion for leave to serve a single early request for admission. The request asked whether Meta filed a CyberTipline report regarding Plaintiff’s account. The court denied the motion.

•	From that denial forward, the defendants in the 376 Action knew what Plaintiff’s discovery would target: the existence or non-existence of a CyberTipline report.

•	The operative complaint in the 376 Action alleged that Meta filed no CyberTipline report. Its prayer sought a declaration that no CyberTipline report was filed regarding the July 4, 2022 enforcement event.

•	On April 9, 2026, Meta moved to dismiss the 376 Action (ECF No. 85). Meta described Plaintiff’s allegation that a CyberTipline report had been submitted and disseminated as “hypothetical (and elsewhere contradicted).” Meta identified the contradiction as Plaintiff’s allegation that “Meta filed no CyberTipline report.”

•	In the 286 Action, the existence or non-existence of a CyberTipline report bore on the claims then pending, including the falsity and factual basis of the statements challenged in that action.

C.	Plaintiff’s Disclosed Survivor Status

•	On September 9, 2025, Plaintiff filed a complaint in Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., et al., Case No. 3:25-cv-07671-CRB (N.D. Cal.) (the “California Action”).

•	That complaint contained a single footnote. The footnote states: “As a CSA survivor, Plaintiff gratefully acknowledges the unwavering support of his wife, whose steady presence made the psychological recovery, and subsequent preparation of this Complaint possible. He further acknowledges his children, especially his eldest, who endured his distance during the preparation of this filing after once celebrating his NRVTA graduation with pride. This work now returns to them, just as their father and husband does.”

•	The footnote disclosed that Plaintiff is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse and had undergone a psychological recovery that made preparation of the complaint possible.

•	Before April 22, 2026, then, Plaintiff had disclosed that he is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse. He had described undergoing psychological recovery. He retained the functional capacity to prepare and prosecute his pending actions.

•	The publicly filed pleadings in the 286 Action disclosed on their face that Plaintiff is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse. Those pleadings alleged that placing Plaintiff’s name near child-sexual-exploitation terminology had already caused Plaintiff emotional injury.

•	Meta, Anderson, and Keegan, through their respective counsel, received and litigated against the 286 Action pleadings containing those disclosures before April 21, 2026.

•	The Kirkland attorneys who appeared for Accenture in the 376 Action also represented Anderson and Keegan in the 286 Action. They therefore possessed the 286 Action pleadings before April 21, 2026. Accenture’s authorized representatives knew of the disclosures before April 21, 2026.

D.	CyberTipline Reporting by Meta-Operated Services

•	NCMEC receives CyberTipline reports from Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp.

E.	Counsel Operating Across Both Actions

•	Fassbender, an attorney at Orrick, was counsel of record for Meta in the 286 Action and for Meta and Genpact Limited in the 376 Action.

•	Chapleau and Anderson, attorneys at Kirkland, were counsel of record for Accenture in the 376 Action. Kirkland, through Chapleau, also represented Anderson and Keegan in the 286 Action.

•	Anderson held two roles at once. In the 286 Action he was an individual defendant and a noticed deposition witness. In the 376 Action he was counsel of record for Accenture.

F.	The Deposition Program

•	On April 7, 2026, Plaintiff served a Rule 30(b)(6) deposition notice on Accenture in the 376 Action. The notice set a two-day examination for April 29 and April 30, 2026. Plaintiff served the notice on Chapleau and Anderson.

•	Matter for Examination No. 5 of that notice is captioned “CyberTipline Reporting and Reportability Status.” It encompasses “whether any CyberTipline Report was Transmitted to NCMEC in connection with the Account-Level Enforcement Event.”

•	On April 7, 2026, Plaintiff noticed Anderson’s deposition in the 286 Action for April 28, 2026. On April 10, 2026, Plaintiff re-served the notice with logistical details.

•	Plaintiff retained a court reporter and a videographer for the noticed depositions.

G.	The April 9, 2026 Transmissions

•	On April 9, 2026, Plaintiff transmitted to NCMEC’s Legal Department a letter captioned “Advance Notice of Intended Subpoenas — Two Separate Matters.” The letter identified the 376 Action and the 286 Action by caption and case number. It enclosed copies of the signed subpoenas Plaintiff intended to serve formally on NCMEC after the notice period had run. It stated that formal service would occur after the notice period had run.

•	Schedule A to each subpoena commanded one item: a document sufficient to show whether NCMEC received or maintains any CyberTipline report concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com. Schedule A expressly excluded the contents of any report.

•	The April 9, 2026 transmission gave NCMEC advance notice of the subpoenas and included copies of the signed subpoenas. Neither subpoena had been formally served on NCMEC. Plaintiff did not request or authorize a response before formal service. Plaintiff did not waive service. Plaintiff did not authorize NCMEC or Hall to treat receipt of the advance-notice package as formal service.

•	On April 9, 2026, Plaintiff served the same materials under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 45(a)(4) on counsel for the parties in both actions, including Orrick for Meta and Kirkland for Accenture.

•	On April 9, 2026, Plaintiff transmitted the advance notice and its enclosures to NCMEC. As of that date, counsel for Meta and counsel for Accenture had received identical materials for their clients. The materials identified the same two federal actions, the same three identifiers, and the same discovery objective. Each recipient knew from the face of the materials that formal service on NCMEC was announced to occur only after the notice period had run.

•	Hall possessed or reviewed the case-specific materials no later than the moment she approved, signed, and authorized transmission of the April 22, 2026 letters.

•	Before preparing the two case-keyed letters, Hall either reviewed the publicly filed pleadings in the 286 Action or received from one or more participants in the two actions case-specific materials reproducing or describing those pleadings. Those materials disclosed that Plaintiff is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse and described the psychological recovery that made preparation of the California Action possible. The source, transmission, and contents of the materials Hall reviewed or received are maintained in Defendants’ records. Plaintiff cannot reach them without discovery.

•	Hall was Corporate Counsel of the federally designated clearinghouse for CyberTipline reporting. She knew what it ordinarily means, in criminal and law-enforcement terms, to associate a named individual with CyberTipline reports.

•	On the same day, April 9, 2026, Meta filed a motion to dismiss and a motion to transfer in the 376 Action.

H.	The April 21, 2026 Filings

•	On April 21, 2026, Meta, Anderson, and Keegan filed a Joint Motion to Stay Discovery and Hold Rule 26(f) Requirements in Abeyance in the 286 Action (ECF No. 49). Chapleau signed for Anderson and Keegan. Fassbender signed for Meta.

•	On April 21, 2026, Anderson and Keegan filed a Time-Sensitive Motion for Protective Order in the 286 Action (ECF No. 50). The motion sought to prevent Anderson’s April 28, 2026 deposition and requested a ruling by April 24, 2026. It stated: “This motion must be decided by April 24 because Plaintiff noticed Anderson’s deposition on April 28, 2026.”

•	On April 21, 2026, Meta, Accenture, TaskUs, Inc., and Genpact Limited filed a Joint Motion to Stay Discovery in the 376 Action (ECF No. 92). Fassbender signed and filed the motion for Meta and Genpact Limited. Chapleau signed with permission for Accenture. The motion recited that Plaintiff had sought leave to serve a Request for Admission relating to “whether Meta filed a CyberTipline report regarding Plaintiff’s account.” It stated that Plaintiff had served “‘advance notices’ and actual notices of specific discovery that Plaintiff intends to seek such as Rule 30(b)(6) depositions and third-party subpoenas.”

•	On April 21, 2026, Accenture filed a Time-Sensitive Motion for Protective Order in the 376 Action (ECF No. 93). The motion sought to prevent the April 29-30, 2026 Rule 30(b)(6) deposition and requested a ruling by April 27, 2026. Accenture attached the deposition notice, including Matter for Examination No. 5, as Exhibit 1. The motion stated: “This time-sensitive motion must be decided by April 27 because Plaintiff noticed Accenture’s deposition for April 29-30.”

•	The April 21, 2026 motions sought relief reaching the Anderson deposition, the Accenture Rule 30(b)(6) deposition, and Plaintiff’s contemplated third-party discovery. Neither court had ruled on any of them.

•	Neither April 21, 2026 joint motion—in the 376 Action or the 286 Action—identified any forthcoming response from NCMEC.

I.	The April 22, 2026 Letters: Issuance Before Formal Service

•	On April 22, 2026, Hall issued two letters on NCMEC letterhead. That was one day after the filings described in Section H. It was thirteen days after Plaintiff transmitted the advance-notice package. It was before formal service of either subpoena. Each letter was keyed by caption to one of the two federal actions. One letter bears on its face the caption “Marvelle Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., et al.,” which identifies Case No. 6:26-cv-00376-AGM-DCI. The other bears on its face the caption “Marvelle Ballentine v. Devin S. Anderson, et al.,” which identifies Case No. 6:26-cv-00286-AGM-DCI. Two letters, each keyed to a separate action, reflect the processing of two separate matters under two specific captions.

•	The two letters are identical in substantive text. This Complaint refers to “the April 22, 2026 letter” to mean the content the two letters share. Each letter identified Plaintiff by the names “Marvelle J. Ballentine” and “Jay Ballentine” and by the email address jaychizza@icloud.com.

•	The letter opened with this sentence: “In response to your subpoena issued April 9, 2026, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (‘NCMEC’) provides its written responses as detailed below.”

•	Neither subpoena had been formally served on NCMEC in connection with Plaintiff. No process server had delivered a subpoena to NCMEC. No subpoena return, proof of service, certificate of service, or process-server affidavit reflecting service of either subpoena on NCMEC existed. No court order required Hall or NCMEC to respond. The announced notice period had not run.

•	When the letters issued, none of the April 21, 2026 motions had been decided. Neither court had ruled on any motion to stay discovery or any motion for protective order. The ruling dates the movants themselves had requested had not arrived: April 24, 2026 in the 286 Action, April 27, 2026 in the 376 Action.

•	Hall did not wait for formal service of any subpoena. Hall did not wait for the courts to rule on the pending motions.

•	Every requested ruling date and every noticed deposition fell after April 22, 2026. The 286 Action ruling date fell two days after the letters issued. The 376 Action ruling date fell five days after. The Anderson deposition was set for April 28, 2026, six days after. The Accenture Rule 30(b)(6) deposition was set for April 29 and 30, 2026, seven and eight days after. No rule, order, or obligation required Hall to issue the letters before any of those dates.

•	On April 27, 2026, the magistrate judge in the 286 Action granted the motion for protective order and temporarily stayed discovery. On April 30, 2026, the magistrate judge in the 376 Action entered a report recommending that the joint motion to stay discovery be granted (ECF No. 103). On May 1, 2026, the magistrate judge in the 376 Action granted Accenture’s motion for protective order and ordered: “Discovery is temporarily stayed pending resolution of the motion to stay discovery” (ECF No. 104).

•	The letter did not produce the document Schedule A described. It stated instead: “NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the present.”

•	The three identifiers stated in the letter were quoted from Plaintiff’s own April 9, 2026 notice.

•	Each letter was addressed to Plaintiff alone, at his commercial mail-receiving address in Alexandria, Virginia. Neither letter bore any notation that it was copied to any court or counsel of record. Neither letter was filed in either action.

•	Neither letter was a CyberTipline report. Neither was a referral or disclosure to any law-enforcement agency. Each letter was voluntary correspondence. It issued after signed subpoenas existed, before formal service of either, and in the absence of any court order or other legal obligation. The challenged conduct was not undertaken as part of any effort to identify a child victim. The conduct alleged was intentional, was undertaken with actual malice and reckless disregard of a substantial risk of injury without legal justification, and served the litigation-directed purpose alleged in Section Q.

•	Hall was NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel when she drafted, signed, and transmitted the letters. She signed both in the course of her work at NCMEC’s Alexandria, Virginia headquarters.

•	As Corporate Counsel, Hall was responsible for legal correspondence NCMEC issued in response to claimed legal process.

•	On information and belief, NCMEC keeps ordinary legal-intake records sufficient to show whether a subpoena has been served on it.

•	On information and belief, Hall reviewed or had access to those records, and they were sufficient to tell her, before issuance, that no subpoena had been served on NCMEC.

•	Hall’s signature appears on each letter. Each letter identifies Hall as the sender.

•	Hall controlled or approved the wording of the letters. Hall selected the language characterizing them as a response to a subpoena. Hall authorized their transmission.

•	Hall drafted and transmitted the letters.

•	Before drafting, signing, and transmitting the letters, Hall reviewed or had access to the docket of Case No. 6:26-cv-00376-AGM-DCI and the docket of Case No. 6:26-cv-00286-AGM-DCI.

•	Hall had reason to know that each docket contained publicly filed claims brought by Plaintiff. Hall had reason to know that the docket of Case No. 6:26-cv-00286-AGM-DCI contained publicly filed claims predicated on the linkage of Plaintiff’s name to child-sexual-exploitation terminology.

•	Hall has not withdrawn, corrected, or retracted either letter. Hall has instead affirmatively defended the letters as accurate and proper.

J.	Souras’s Legal Responsibilities and Participation in the April 22 Responses

•	Souras was NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer before April 22, 2026 and on that date. NCMEC’s biography of Souras, submitted to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce with her testimony of March 26, 2025, states that as Chief Legal Officer she manages NCMEC’s legal operations relating to its mission. NCMEC’s published leadership profile states that Souras is responsible for all legal affairs of NCMEC, including oversight of contractual, litigation, compliance, governance, and intellectual property matters.

•	The same NCMEC profile states that Souras advises NCMEC’s President and Chief Executive Officer and NCMEC staff on legal issues, provides counsel to NCMEC’s Board of Directors, and serves as assistant corporate secretary to the Board. The March 2025 biography states that she collaborates on civil and criminal legal issues relating to online child sexual exploitation with technology companies, prosecutors, defense counsel, and private attorneys.

•	Souras has performed those functions in litigation concerning CyberTipline reports. In United States v. Rosenschein, No. 1:16-cr-04571-JCH (D.N.M.), the court’s memorandum opinion and order of June 18, 2020 (Doc. 251, at 8) described emails showing that a detective sent Souras, as NCMEC’s general counsel, the defendant’s discovery request and motion to suppress; that Souras forwarded the suppression motion to the attorney for a technology company; and that government counsel emailed Souras hash values and file names associated with the two CyberTipline reports in that case, which Souras sent to an NCMEC vice president.

•	On March 26, 2025, Souras testified before the House Committee on Energy and Commerce as NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer. Her written testimony addressed Meta’s CyberTipline reporting, identified Meta as historically the largest reporter to the CyberTipline, addressed the information that CyberTipline reports contain, and stated that NCMEC can share elements of CyberTipline reports only with law enforcement and entities meeting statutory requirements.

•	On July 20, 2026, NCMEC published a description of a Senior Counsel position within its Office of Legal Counsel. The description states that the position provides strategic partnership to the Chief Legal Officer and helps ensure that written materials and work product reviewed or issued by the Office of Legal Counsel are accurate, well-sourced, and consistent with NCMEC’s positions.

•	Before joining NCMEC in 2006, Souras practiced as an associate at Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP. Orrick represented Meta in the 376 Action and the 286 Action and received Plaintiff’s April 9, 2026 materials on Meta’s behalf, as alleged in Sections E and G.

•	On April 9, 2026, Plaintiff transmitted the advance-notice package by overnight mail to NCMEC, addressed to “Legal Department / Subpoena Compliance.” The package identified the 376 Action and the 286 Action by caption and case number, enclosed signed copies of the two subpoenas, and stated that formal service would follow after the notice period had run. Section G alleges the package.
